title: A House of Prayer for All Peoples
sum: The last part of Isaiah opens with a surprise. To people who keep justice and the Sabbath, the LORD promises a place in his house, and he names two groups who feared they had none: foreigners who have joined themselves to him, and eunuchs who could have no children. The foreigners will bring sacrifices to his altar, and the eunuchs will have "a marker and a name" better than sons and daughters. The temple will be "a house of prayer for all the peoples" (56:7), the line Jesus quoted when he cleared the temple courts.

Then the tone turns. The LORD calls wild animals to feed on his people, because their watchmen are blind and their shepherds are greedy drunks (56:9–12). The charge runs on into chapter 57. These two halves set the pattern of chapters 56–66: a wide welcome for all who hold to the LORD, and a sharp judgment on those inside Israel who do not.
readings: Read as a welcome

The chapter widens the people of God. Faith and faithfulness, not ancestry or the body, decide who belongs. Jews have read it of converts, and Christians of the church of Jews and gentiles (Acts 8; Ephesians 2:11–22).
Read as a community debate

Many critical scholars hear one side of an argument in Judah after the return. Some leaders, like Ezra and Nehemiah later, kept foreigners out; this prophet answers that foreigners who keep covenant belong. The blind watchmen of 56:10 may be the very leaders who were shutting people out.
Read as the frame of a book

The chapter's opening, "keep justice and practice righteousness", and its closing hope for all nations echo chapter 1 and chapter 2 (1:17; 2:2–4). Childs and others see 56:1–8 as a gateway that shows how the whole book is to be read: the promise to the nations is kept for those who do righteousness.

views.H: The chapter fits the years after Cyrus let the exiles go home (538 BC) and before or during the rebuilding of the temple (520–515 BC), when the community argued over who belonged. Foreigners and eunuchs were real people in Judah then: some had married into Judean families or served in foreign courts. The "house" of 56:5–7 assumes a temple and altar, either rebuilt or about to be.
views.C: Most critical scholars see 56–66 as a collection from prophets in Judah after 538, building on the message of 40–55 (the gathering of 56:8 echoes 40:11 and 43:5–7). Some see it as a deliberate counterweight to the stricter rules of Ezekiel 44 and Ezra–Nehemiah. Those who hold to a single author read it as Isaiah addressing a future generation, in line with his own vision of nations streaming to Zion (2:2–4).
views.J: Rashi and Kimchi read the "foreigner who has joined himself" as the convert, the ger tsedeq, and the passage became a classic text for welcoming converts. The phrase "gathers the banished of Israel" entered the daily Amidah. The name of Israel's Holocaust memorial, Yad Vashem, comes from 56:5.
views.X: The New Testament sees the prophecy fulfilled as the gospel reaches outsiders: Jesus quotes 56:7 in the temple (Mark 11:17), Philip baptizes an Ethiopian eunuch reading Isaiah (Acts 8:26–39), and Paul speaks of gentiles brought near (Ephesians 2:13–19). Many Christians also read 56:4–5 as comfort for those who are childless or single for the kingdom's sake (Matthew 19:12).
views.F: Some readers who expect a rebuilt temple in a future kingdom (Ezekiel 40–48) read 56:6–7 of the sacrifices of foreigners there; others read it as fulfilled in Christ and the church.

deep.h: The witnesses behind the notes on Isaiah 56–66
deep.b: The text notes and variants in these chapters rest on three sources read directly. The Hebrew is the Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), with its written text (Ketiv) and its reading tradition (Qere). The Dead Sea Scrolls were checked in the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcription of the Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a), the second Cave 1 scroll (1QIsa-b, 1Q8) and the Cave 4 copies where they survive; only letters on the leather are cited, never letters the editors restored. The Greek is Swete's edition (Codex Vaticanus). The Targum, Ziegler's critical Greek text, the Vulgate and the rabbinic and church writers are cited from editions and commentaries, as named in each note.

deep.h: Who may come in? Deuteronomy, Ezekiel, Ezra and Isaiah 56
deep.b:
Israel's law did not have one rule for all foreigners. A resident foreigner (ger) who was circumcised could eat the Passover (Exodus 12:48), and Ruth the Moabite became David's great-grandmother. But Deuteronomy 23:1–8 kept eunuchs, Ammonites and Moabites out of "the assembly of the LORD", and Ezekiel 44:6–9 condemned bringing "foreigners, uncircumcised in heart and flesh" into the sanctuary. Nehemiah read Deuteronomy 23 aloud and "set apart from Israel all the mixed crowd" (Nehemiah 13:3), using the same verb badal, "separate", that the foreigner fears in 56:3.

Isaiah 56 does not argue with these laws directly. It sets a condition instead: the foreigner and the eunuch who keep the Sabbath, choose what pleases God and hold to his covenant will have a place in his house. Some scholars see a real clash of views inside the community after the exile (Hanson; Blenkinsopp). Others think the laws and the prophecy address different cases: outsiders who brought their own gods, and outsiders who had taken the LORD as God. Either way, the book that began with Jerusalem's sin ends with the nations coming to worship (66:18–23).

settings.what: An oracle welcoming foreigners and eunuchs
settings.to: The community of Judah and those gathering to it: returned exiles, foreigners who had joined them, and eunuchs who feared they were shut out
settings.when: After the return from Babylon in 538 BC, when the people argued about who belonged and the temple was being rebuilt or newly in use (critical view); or foreseen by Isaiah in the 700s BC for that later day (traditional view)
settings.why: To widen the circle of God's people: those who hold to the covenant and the Sabbath belong, whatever their birth or body. The words were meant to reassure the outsiders and to correct insiders who would shut them out. Knowing that some in the community wanted a stricter line (Nehemiah 13:1–3) shows how bold the promise was.
settings.readers: For later readers of the whole book, the oracle turns the promise of nations coming to Zion (2:2–4) into a present invitation, and it frames the last chapters, which end with foreigners serving as priests (66:21).
views: A prophet in Judah after 538 BC, speaking in a community divided over foreigners and worship (Duhm; Westermann; Blenkinsopp).
Isaiah son of Amoz, writing in Hezekiah's day for a future generation after the exile (Young; Oswalt; Motyer).

settings.what: A charge against the leaders and the idol worshipers
settings.by: The prophet, speaking for the LORD
settings.to: Judah's leaders, its "watchmen" and "shepherds", and the people who worship other gods
settings.when: Debated: in the community after the exile (critical view), or in the idolatry of Manasseh's reign before it (some traditional and some critical scholars)
settings.why: To expose leaders who sleep, drink and profit while the people are torn apart, and so to explain why the promised salvation has not come. The call to wild animals in 56:9 is a summons to judgment.
views: The leaders are the community's own officials and prophets in the 500s or 400s BC (Westermann; Hanson).
The leaders and the rites of 57:3–13 fit the idolatry of the 600s BC, so some see an older oracle placed here (Blenkinsopp discusses this; Oswalt reads it as Isaiah's own).

title: High and Holy, With the Crushed
sum: Chapter 57 begins with good people dying unnoticed and goes on to the darkest charge in these chapters. The LORD calls the people "sons of a fortune-teller" and accuses them of rites under the trees, children slaughtered in the ravines, sacred stones chosen as their "share", and a bed spread for other gods on the high hills. They courted "the king" with oil and sent envoys as deep as Sheol. Their gods will be blown away like a breath, but whoever takes refuge in the LORD will inherit the land (57:13).

Then a voice calls for the road to be cleared, and the LORD speaks one of the best-loved sayings of the book: he lives "in the height and in holiness", and also with the crushed and lowly in spirit, to bring them back to life (57:15). His anger will not last forever. He will heal, lead and comfort, and he offers peace to those far and near. Only the wicked, restless as the sea, have no peace.
readings: Read as a sermon against idolatry
The chapter uses the oldest charges in the prophets: worship under trees, child sacrifice, idolatry as adultery. It shows how deep the old sins ran, and why the promised restoration still waits.
Read as a word of comfort
The judgment of 57:3–13 is the dark background for 57:14–21. God's last word is not anger but healing, and the lowly, not the powerful, are where he chooses to live.
Read as two communities

Some scholars hear in 57:1–2 and 57:13 a faithful group, "the righteous" and "the one who shelters in me", set against a majority who practice the old rites. On this reading, chapters 56–66 reflect a split in the community that will become sharper in chapters 65–66.

views.H: The rites described here, sacrifice of children, worship of the dead, offerings on high hills, fit the religion Jeremiah and Ezekiel condemned before 586 BC. If the passage comes from after the return, it shows such practices continuing among people who never went into exile; if before, it may be an older oracle placed here.
views.C: Critics are divided on 57:3–13. Some date it before the exile (Westermann), others see it as the prophet's description of opponents in the community after 538, drawing on older language (Hanson; Schramm; Blenkinsopp). 57:14–21 is generally seen as a deliberate reuse of 40:1–11 and 48:22.
views.J: The synagogue reads 57:14–58:14 on the morning of the Day of Atonement. The Talmud draws from 57:15 that God lives with the humble, and from 57:19 that one who repents stands higher than the completely righteous (Berakhot 34b).
views.X: Christians have read 57:15 as a description of God's nearness to the contrite and as a picture of the incarnation, the high God dwelling with the lowly (compare Philippians 2:5–8). Paul uses 57:19 for the peace Christ makes between Jews and gentiles (Ephesians 2:17).
views.F: Those who read Isaiah's restoration as still to come see in 57:13, "inherit the land", a promise not yet completely kept, joined to the new heavens and new earth of 65–66.

deep.h: Rites of the dead and the high places
deep.b:
Many details in 57:3–13 are hard to pin down, and scholars have proposed several settings. The "smooth stones of the ravine" (57:6), the "reminder" behind the doorpost (57:8), the trip "to the king" and the envoys sent "as deep as Sheol" (57:9) have all been read as signs of a cult of the dead: offerings to dead ancestors in the valleys, the god of the underworld, and perhaps the god Molech. The Hebrew Bible elsewhere condemns consulting the dead (Deuteronomy 18:11; Isaiah 8:19) and eating "the sacrifices of the dead" (Psalm 106:28).

Others read most of the language as picture: the bed, the lovers and the perfume are the prophets' way of describing Israel's unfaithfulness, as in Ezekiel 16 and 23. Both can be true. The prophet describes real religious practices in the language of a betrayed marriage, so that the reader feels the betrayal, not just the error.

echoes: 6:1; 40:3; 48:22; 52:13; 62:10; 66:2; Deuteronomy 6:9; Deuteronomy 12:2; 2 Kings 21:6; 2 Kings 22:20; Psalm 34:18; Psalm 51:17; Psalm 103:9; Matthew 5:3–5; Ephesians 2:17; Hebrews 13:15

settings.what: The LORD's word of healing for the lowly
settings.by: A voice (57:14), then the LORD, "the One who is high and lifted up"
settings.to: The people of God, especially the crushed and lowly among them, and the exiles still far away
settings.when: Directly after the charge of 56:9–57:13, as its answer
settings.why: To promise that God's anger has a limit. He will clear the road, heal the sinner who keeps turning away, and give peace to far and near. The words turn the judgment into hope, but they draw a line: the wicked will not have peace. Knowing that 57:14 reuses the road of 40:3 shows that the prophet sees the old promise of return still unfinished, blocked now by the people's own sins.
settings.readers: In the synagogue these words begin the reading for the Day of Atonement, so they have been heard for centuries as a call to repentance with the promise of healing.
views: Words to a disappointed community in Judah, where the return had not brought the glory 40–55 promised (Westermann; Blenkinsopp).
Isaiah's word to the faithful of a later day, set after the charge against Manasseh-style idolatry (Oswalt; Motyer).

title: The Fast the LORD Chooses
sum: The prophet is told to shout like a ram's horn: the people who seek God every day and fast faithfully are in rebellion. They complain that God ignores their fasting. He answers that on their fast days they pursue their business, drive their workers, and quarrel and fight. A bowed head and a bed of sackcloth are not the fast he wants.

The fast God chooses is to break the chains of the oppressed, share bread with the hungry, take in the uprooted and clothe the naked (58:6–7). Then their light will break out like the dawn, God will answer "I am here", and they will rebuild the ruins of the city. The chapter ends with the Sabbath: if they stop their own business on God's holy day and call it a delight, God will be their delight and give them Jacob's inheritance.
readings: Read as prophetic ethics

The chapter is one of the Bible's clearest statements that worship and justice belong together. Religious practice is not wrong; it is empty when it goes with oppression. Many social reformers have taken 58:6–7 as their charter.
Read as a liturgy

Some scholars see the chapter as a prophetic answer to a community fast-day liturgy, perhaps one of the fasts mourning Jerusalem's fall (Zechariah 7–8). The people's complaint in 58:3 may quote their actual lament.
Read as a whole with 56
The Sabbath frames chapters 56–58 (56:2–6; 58:13–14). Keeping the Sabbath and doing justice are the two marks of those who belong, whether Israelites or foreigners.

views.H: Fasting became central after 586 BC: four yearly fasts mourned the siege, the fall of the city, the burning of the temple and the murder of Gedaliah (Zechariah 7:3–5; Zechariah 8:19). Nehemiah 5:1–5 shows Judeans losing fields and children to their own richer neighbors in the 400s BC, the kind of oppression 58:3–7 condemns.
views.C: Most critics date the chapter to the decades after 538 BC and read it as a prophetic sermon on a fast-day question, like Zechariah 7. The Sabbath verses (58:13–14) are often thought to be a slightly later addition that ties the chapter to 56:1–8.
views.J: The synagogue reads 57:14–58:14 on the morning of the Day of Atonement, the holiest fast of the year, so that the people hear, while fasting, that God wants justice and mercy. The rabbis drew the customs of Sabbath delight, Sabbath speech and Sabbath meals from 58:13–14.
views.X: Christian churches read Isaiah 58 at the start of Lent, often on Ash Wednesday, to set fasting beside almsgiving and justice. Luke 4:18 includes 58:6 in Jesus' reading at Nazareth. Jesus' teaching on fasting in secret (Matthew 6:16–18) and his judgment scene (Matthew 25:31–46) carry the same message.
views.F: Some read 58:12 and 58:14, the rebuilt ruins and the heights of the land, as promises still waiting for a restored Israel.

deep.h: Fasting in the Bible and after
deep.b:
The law of Moses commands only one fast, the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29–31), though people fasted at other times in grief, danger or repentance (2 Samuel 12:16; Esther 4:16; Joel 2:12). After the exile the fasts of mourning grew (Zechariah 8:19), and by Jesus' day pious Jews fasted twice a week (Luke 18:12). Isaiah 58 does not cancel fasting. It defines it: a fast pleases God when the hunger of the one fasting leads to feeding the hungry, and when humbling oneself before God goes with freeing others.

Jewish and Christian teachers kept this link. The Mishnah tells how, on public fast days, the elders read Jonah's lesson that God saw what Nineveh did, not their sackcloth (Mishnah Taanit 2:1, citing Jonah 3:10). The Epistle of Barnabas (3:1–5), an early Christian writing, quotes Isaiah 58:4–10 at length as God's word on fasting, and the Shepherd of Hermas tells believers to give what they save by fasting to the poor (Similitude 5.3). Both traditions heard Isaiah 58 as the measure of a true fast.
deep.refs: 58:3–7; Leviticus 16:29–31; Zechariah 7:3–10; Zechariah 8:19; Jonah 3:10; Luke 18:12; Matthew 6:16–18

echoes: 1:11–17; 52:12; 61:1–2; Leviticus 16:29–31; Deuteronomy 32:13; Jeremiah 34:8–17; Zechariah 7:3–10; Ezekiel 18:7; Amos 5:21–24; Micah 6:6–8; Matthew 6:16–18; Matthew 25:35–36; Luke 4:18

settings.what: A sermon on the true fast and the Sabbath
settings.by: The LORD, who sends the prophet to speak like a ram's horn
settings.to: "My people... the house of Jacob": worshipers in Judah who fasted faithfully and complained that God did not notice, among them employers and creditors who oppressed the poor
settings.when: A fast day, or a season of fasting, after the fall of Jerusalem, most likely in the years after the return when the city still lay in ruins (critical view); or Isaiah's word for that future day (traditional view)
settings.why: To answer the people's complaint (58:3) and redirect their piety. God has not ignored their fasting; he rejects a fast that goes with oppression. The sermon promises that justice will bring God's answer, light, healing and the rebuilding of the ruins. Knowing that the hearers were sincere, regular worshipers makes the words sharper: the warning is for the devout, not the careless.
settings.readers: For later readers the chapter became the measure of all religious practice. Its place in the Day of Atonement service, and in the Lenten lectionaries of many churches, shows how both synagogue and church heard it as addressed to themselves.
views: A sermon to the community in Judah in the late 500s or 400s BC, close to Zechariah 7–8 and Nehemiah 5 (Westermann; Blenkinsopp).
Isaiah's sermon, perhaps first aimed at the hypocrisy of his own day and kept for later generations (Oswalt; Motyer).

traditions.q: Isaiah promises blessing to those who keep the Sabbath and call it a delight (58:13–14), foreigners included (56:2–6). Does this bind Christians, and on which day?
views: Yes. The seventh-day Sabbath was made at creation and is kept in the Ten Commandments, and Isaiah's promise to foreigners who keep it shows that it was always meant for all peoples (Fundamental Beliefs 20). Seventh-day Adventists treat 58:13 as a guide for keeping the day, from sunset Friday to sunset Saturday, free of business and personal pursuits.

The Sabbath principle still binds, but on the first day of the week, the Lord's Day. The Westminster Confession says the day is to be kept holy by rest "from their own works, words, and thoughts about their worldly employments and recreations", and cites Isaiah 58:13 for it (21.8).

Sunday fulfills the Sabbath for Christians, and the Church applies the spirit of Isaiah 58 to it: Catholics are to worship at Mass and avoid work and business that hinder worship, joy and works of mercy (Catechism 2175–2176, 2184–2186).

The Sabbath law of Moses no longer binds the conscience; the church keeps Sunday for good order and to hear God's word (Augsburg Confession 28). Luther explained the commandment as holding preaching and God's word sacred and gladly hearing and learning it.

Most Baptists keep the first day as the Lord's Day in memory of the resurrection, devoted to worship and rest (Baptist Faith and Message, article 8). Seventh Day Baptists, an older and smaller body, keep Saturday as Isaiah's Sabbath.

title: No One Stepped In
sum: Chapter 59 answers the question behind chapter 58: why has God not saved? It is not that his hand is too short or his ear too dull. The people's wrongdoings have split them off from him. The prophet lists the sins: bloodstained hands, lying lips, dishonest courts, schemes like viper's eggs and spider's webs, feet that run to shed innocent blood. Paul quotes 59:7–8 in Romans 3.

Then the people speak: justice is far from us, we grope like the blind, we growl like bears. They confess their rebellions (59:12–13). The LORD sees that there is no justice and no one to step in, so he acts himself, putting on righteousness as armor and salvation as a helmet. He will repay his enemies, and the nations from west to east will fear him. A redeemer will come to Zion for those who turn from rebellion, and God makes a covenant: his spirit and his words will never leave his people's mouth.
readings: Read as a liturgy

Many scholars see a liturgy of lament in three parts: accusation (59:1–8), communal confession (59:9–15a) and God's answer (59:15b–21). Similar movements appear in the Psalms and in Ezra 9 and Nehemiah 9.
Read as the divine warrior

59:15b–20 is one of the Bible's pictures of God as a warrior, like Exodus 15:3 and Psalm 98:1. It prepares for 63:1–6 and for the rider on the white horse in Revelation 19:11–16. God's war is against injustice, and he fights alone.
Read through Paul
Christians have read the chapter through Romans: 59:7–8 shows that all are under sin (Romans 3:15–17), and 59:20–21 promises that the deliverer will save Israel (Romans 11:26–27).

views.H: The chapter fits a community where courts were corrupt and the strong preyed on the weak, as Nehemiah 5 describes Judah in the 400s BC. The people's lament that the promised salvation had not come matches the disappointment of the years after 538, when the temple was rebuilt but Judah stayed poor and ruled by Persia.
views.C: Most critics read the chapter as a composite liturgy from Third Isaiah's circle. The divine warrior passage (59:15b–20) is closely tied to 63:1–6, and the two may frame chapters 60–62. 59:21 is often seen as a prose addition that links the prophet's words to later generations.
views.J: The Targum renders 59:20 "A redeemer will come to Zion" and Jewish tradition reads it of the Messiah. 59:20–21 opens the prayer U-va le-Tsiyyon, recited every morning, which asks God to keep his covenant of spirit and word with Israel and its children.
views.X: The church has read 59:17 with Ephesians 6:14–17 as the armor of God, and 59:20 with Romans 11:26 as the promise of Christ's coming as deliverer of Israel. Christians differ on whether Romans 11:26 means a future turning of the Jewish people to Christ (see below).
views.F: Futurist readers hold that 59:20 and Romans 11:26 will be fulfilled when Christ returns and Israel as a people turns to him, often linked with Zechariah 12:10.

deep.b:
Paul ends his long argument about Israel in Romans 9–11 with a mystery: a partial hardening has come on Israel until the full number of the gentiles has come in, "and in this way all Israel will be saved" (Romans 11:25–26). He backs it with Isaiah 59:20–21 and 27:9 in their Greek form. What "all Israel" means has been argued for centuries. Some read it as the Jewish people as a whole at the end of the age, turning to their Messiah; others as the whole people of God, Jews and gentiles together; others as the full number of Jews who believe through history.

Isaiah's own verse speaks of a redeemer for "those in Jacob who turn from rebellion", a repentant people within Israel. Paul's Greek text says the deliverer himself "will turn away ungodliness from Jacob". Paul's reading stresses God's initiative and mercy (Romans 11:29–32), which suits his argument that God has not rejected his people (Romans 11:1–2).

echoes: 50:2; 53:12; 63:1–6; Numbers 11:23; Proverbs 1:16; Ezekiel 22:30; Romans 3:15–17; Romans 11:26–27; Ephesians 6:14–17; 1 Thessalonians 5:8; Revelation 19:11–16

settings.what: The prophet's accusation and the people's confession
settings.by: The prophet (59:1–8), then the people, or the prophet speaking for them, as "we" (59:9–15)
settings.to: The community in Judah who complained that God did not save or hear them; in 59:9–15 the people speak to God
settings.when: In a time of disappointment when the promised restoration seemed delayed: after the return, in the critical view; or foreseen by Isaiah for a later generation, in the traditional view
settings.why: To show that the delay of salvation is not God's weakness but the people's sin, and to lead them from complaint to confession. Hearing the people say "we" changes the tone: the charge is taken up as their own prayer.
settings.readers: Paul's use of 59:7–8 (Romans 3:15–17) made this charge part of the Christian teaching that all have sinned.
views: A prophetic liturgy used in worship after the exile, with accusation, confession and divine answer (Westermann; Blenkinsopp).
One sermon by the prophet who speaks first to the people and then for them (Oswalt; Motyer).

settings.what: The LORD arms himself to save, and a covenant
settings.by: The prophet describes the LORD (59:15–19); then the LORD speaks (59:20–21)
settings.to: The same community, especially "those in Jacob who turn from rebellion"
settings.when: As God's answer to the confession
settings.why: To assure the penitent that God himself will act when no human leader will, judging the oppressors and coming to Zion as redeemer. The covenant of 59:21 promises that God's spirit and words will stay with them and their children. Knowing that the hearers had just confessed their sin makes this a word of forgiveness, not only of judgment.
settings.readers: For Paul, writing to the church at Rome, 59:20–21 was the scriptural ground for hope that God would still save Israel (Romans 11:26–27).

traditions.q: Paul cites 59:20 to say that "all Israel will be saved" (Romans 11:26). Does this promise a future turning of the Jewish people to Christ?
views: The Church teaches that Christ's glorious return waits on his recognition by "all Israel", citing Romans 11:20–26, and that the Jewish people remain dear to God, whose gifts and call are irrevocable (Catechism 674, 839; Nostra Aetate 4).

Divided. Calvin read "all Israel" as the whole people of God, Jews and gentiles, gathered in through history. Many Puritans and later Reformed writers, including Charles Hodge, expected a large future turning of the Jewish people to Christ before the end.

Yes. After the church age God will turn again to national Israel; at Christ's return the surviving Jewish people will repent and be saved, and the promises of 59:20–21 will be kept to Israel as a nation in the millennial kingdom.

title: Rise Up and Shine
sum: Chapter 60 is a poem of light spoken to Zion as a woman. Darkness covers the earth, but the LORD's glory dawns over her, and nations and kings walk toward her light. Her sons and daughters come home from far away; the wealth of the sea and of the nations is turned toward her. Camels from Midian and Sheba bring gold and frankincense, Arab flocks come for her altar, and the Tarshish ships carry her children with silver and gold.

Foreigners rebuild her walls, her gates stand open day and night, and those who crushed her bow at her feet and call her the City of the LORD. Bronze becomes gold, peace becomes her governor, and violence is gone. In the end the sun and moon are not needed, for the LORD is her light forever. Her people will all be righteous, "the sprout of my planting", and the smallest will become a mighty nation.
readings: Read as the restoration of Jerusalem

For its first hearers, the poem promised that the ruined, half-empty city of the return would become the center of the world: its exiles home, its temple adorned, its walls rebuilt, its enemies at peace. Some of this, such as the rebuilding of the walls, came in a modest form under Persian rule.
Read as the new Jerusalem

Revelation 21–22 draws on chapter 60 more than on any other passage: the light of the nations, the gates never shut, the glory of the kings, no need of sun or moon. Christians have read the chapter as a picture of the church and of the city to come.
Read in the synagogue
Jews read chapter 60 as one of the seven consolations after the Ninth of Av, and the rabbis drew from it the hope of the messianic age and the world to come (60:21–22).

views.H: After 538 BC Jerusalem was small and poor, with broken walls and a modest temple (Haggai 2:3; Nehemiah 1:3). The chapter answers that reality with a vision of the city's glory. The rebuilding of the temple (515 BC) and the walls (about 445 BC) under Persian sponsorship were partial fulfillments; the full picture far exceeded them.
views.C: Chapters 60–62 are widely seen as the core of Third Isaiah, closest in tone to 40–55 and perhaps the oldest part of 56–66 (Westermann; Zimmerli). The poem reuses 49:14–26 heavily. Many critics take 60:12 and some other lines as later additions.
views.J: Rabbinic tradition read the chapter of the messianic age: 60:21 opens Mishnah Sanhedrin 10, and 60:22 is the text of the Talmud's teaching on hastening the redemption (Sanhedrin 98a). The chapter is the haftarah of Ki Tavo, the sixth of the seven consolations.
views.X: The church reads 60:1–6 at Epiphany, the feast of the magi and the revelation of Christ to the nations, and hears the gold and frankincense of 60:6 in Matthew 2:11. Revelation 21:23–26 and 22:5 make the chapter a picture of the new Jerusalem.
views.F: Futurist readers expect a literal restored Jerusalem in a coming kingdom, to which the nations bring their wealth (compare Zechariah 14:16). Others read the chapter as fulfilled in the new creation of Revelation 21–22.

deep.b:
John's vision of the new Jerusalem borrows the language of Isaiah 60 at point after point. The table below sets them side by side.

Isaiah 60Revelation 21–22
Nations walk toward your light (60:3)The nations will walk by its light (21:24)
Your gates will stand open all the time; day and night they will not be shut (60:11)Its gates will never be shut by day, for there will be no night there (21:25)
The wealth of nations can be brought to you, with their kings led in (60:11)The kings of the earth bring their glory into it; they will bring the glory and honor of the nations into it (21:24, 26)
No longer will the sun be your light... The LORD will be your light forever (60:19)The city does not need the sun or the moon... the glory of God gives it light (21:23; 22:5)
Those who crushed you will bow at your feet (60:14)Those from the synagogue of Satan will bow down at your feet (3:9)

John also changes the picture. Isaiah's city has a temple adorned with Lebanon's timber (60:13); John's has no temple, "because the Lord God, the Almighty, is its temple, and so is the Lamb" (Revelation 21:22). The gifts of the nations are no longer rams for the altar but their "glory and honor".

settings.what: A poem of light for Zion
settings.by: The LORD, through the prophet ("my altar", "my splendid house", 60:7)
settings.to: Zion, spoken to as a woman, and through her the people of Jerusalem: a small, poor community among ruins, whose children were still scattered
settings.when: After the return from Babylon, when the city lay largely in ruins and the promises of 40–55 seemed unfulfilled (critical view); or Isaiah's vision for that time (traditional view)
settings.why: To lift a discouraged people's eyes: their darkness is about to end, God's glory is rising over them, and the nations who once plundered them will come to give. Knowing how small and poor the city was makes the poem's splendor a deliberate act of hope, not a description.
settings.readers: Later readers heard the poem as a vision beyond any rebuilding they saw: in Judaism, the messianic age and the world to come; in Christianity, the church gathered from the nations and the new Jerusalem of Revelation.
views: Spoken in Jerusalem in the late 500s BC, perhaps before the temple was finished in 515 (Westermann; Blenkinsopp).
Isaiah's vision of the far future, given in the 700s BC (Oswalt; Motyer).

title: Good News for the Humble
sum: An unnamed speaker says that the Spirit of the Lord GOD is on him, because the LORD has anointed him. He is sent to bring good news to the humble poor, to bandage broken hearts, to proclaim release to captives and freedom to prisoners, to announce a year of the LORD's goodwill and a day of his vengeance, and to comfort those who mourn in Zion with a garland in place of ashes.

The rest of the chapter describes what follows. The ruins are rebuilt, foreigners tend Israel's flocks, and Israel itself is called the priests of the LORD. Shame gives way to a double share, and God makes an everlasting covenant with his people. The chapter ends with a song of joy from someone dressed like a bride and bridegroom, and a promise that righteousness will sprout like a garden before the nations.
readings: Read as the prophet's call
Many scholars read 61:1–3 as the prophet of 56–66 describing his own mission in words borrowed from the servant passages (42:1–7; 49:1–9). The Targum begins "The prophet said".
Read as the servant or the Messiah

Others hear the servant of the LORD himself, or a messianic figure anointed with the Spirit like the shoot of Jesse (11:1–2). The Qumran texts 11QMelchizedek and 4Q521 already read the passage of a coming deliverer.
Read through Luke 4
For Christian readers, the chapter is Jesus' own description of his work: he reads it at Nazareth and says it is fulfilled today.

views.H: After the return from exile, many Judeans were poor, in debt and dependent on others (Nehemiah 5:1–5). A proclamation of release, modeled on the jubilee (Leviticus 25), would speak directly to that need. Persian-era Judah had no king, so an "anointed" figure who speaks rather than rules fits a prophet.
views.C: Chapters 60–62 are often seen as the heart of Third Isaiah, and 61:1–3 as its programmatic statement. The passage reuses 40–55: the Spirit (42:1), the release of prisoners (42:7; 49:9), good news (40:9; 52:7), comfort (40:1). Some critics think the speaker sees himself as the heir of the servant.
views.J: Jewish reading takes the speaker as the prophet, and the chapter's last verses begin the haftarah of Nitzavim, 61:10–63:9 (the reading runs into chapter 63), the last of the seven consolations before Rosh Hashanah.
views.X: Luke 4:16–21 makes 61:1–2 the opening statement of Jesus' ministry. The church reads the passage at ordinations and in Advent, and the Roman Catholic Chrism Mass uses it for the blessing of holy oils.
views.F: Futurist readers often divide the passage between Christ's first coming (the year of favor) and his second (the day of vengeance), reading the comma where Jesus stopped as a gap of centuries.

deep.h: Isaiah 61 at Qumran and in Luke
deep.b:
Before Jesus, the Qumran community already read Isaiah 61 as a picture of the last days. In 11QMelchizedek (11Q13), the heavenly figure Melchizedek proclaims "release" to the captives in the final jubilee, and the text speaks of "the year of Melchizedek's favor" and a "day of vengeance". In 4Q521, the "Messianic Apocalypse", the Lord, when his messiah appears, will free prisoners, give sight to the blind, heal the wounded, give life to the dead and bring good news to the humble. The list is close to Jesus' answer to John the Baptist (Matthew 11:5).

Luke's version of the reading, set beside Isaiah, shows what was kept and what changed:

Isaiah 61:1–2 (Hebrew)Luke 4:18–19 (following the Greek)
The Spirit of the Lord GOD is on meThe Spirit of the Lord is on me
to bring good news to the humbleto bring good news to the poor
to bandage the broken in heart(lacking in the oldest manuscripts of Luke)
to proclaim release to the captivesto proclaim release to the captives
and an opening wide for those who are boundand sight again for the blind
(from 58:6) to send the crushed away freeto send the crushed away free
a year of the LORD's goodwilla year of the Lord's welcome
and a day of our God's vengeance(not read)

The phrase "to heal the broken in heart" is in later manuscripts of Luke and in the KJV, but not in the oldest ones. The line from 58:6 links the two passages by the word "release" (Greek aphesis).

settings.what: The anointed speaker's mission, and Zion's answer
settings.by: An anointed speaker, perhaps the prophet (61:1–3); the LORD (61:8–9); Zion or the restored people (61:10–11)
settings.to: The mourners of Zion: poor, indebted and discouraged people among the ruins of Judah
settings.when: After the return from Babylon, in the late 500s or early 400s BC (critical view); or Isaiah's vision of that age (traditional view)
settings.why: To announce that the time of release has come: God will free his people as the jubilee freed slaves, rebuild what is ruined, and honor them before the nations. The good news is addressed to the poor and the grieving, not to the powerful.
settings.readers: At Qumran and in the early church the passage was read of the end time and of the Messiah. In Luke, Jesus reads it at Nazareth, claims it as fulfilled, and stops before "a day of vengeance".
views: The anointed speaker is the prophet of 56–66, describing his own call (Westermann; Blenkinsopp).
The speaker is the servant of 40–55 or the coming Messiah (Oswalt; Motyer).

title: Zion's New Name
sum: A voice refuses to keep silent until Zion's righteousness shines out like a torch. The nations will see her glory, and she will receive a new name from the LORD's own mouth. She will be a crown in his hand. No longer will she be called Abandoned or Desolate: her name will be My Delight Is in Her (Hephzibah) and her land Married (Beulah), for God rejoices over her like a bridegroom over his bride.

Guards are posted on Jerusalem's walls, and those who keep the LORD reminded are told to give him no rest until he makes the city firm. God swears that enemies will never again eat Zion's harvest. The chapter ends with a call to go out through the gates and build the road, an announcement to the ends of the earth that Zion's salvation is coming, and four new names: the Holy People, the Redeemed of the LORD, Wanted, and A City Not Abandoned.
readings: Read as a prayer for Jerusalem
The chapter models persistent intercession: those on the walls are to remind God day and night until he keeps his word. It has been used in prayers for Jerusalem in both Jewish and Christian worship.
Read as a wedding
The marriage images of 61:10 and 62:4–5 make the restoration a wedding between God and his people, an image taken up for Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:25–27; Revelation 19:7).

views.H: In the years after the return, Jerusalem was thinly populated and its walls were down until Nehemiah rebuilt them (Nehemiah 1:3; Nehemiah 7:4). The fear of enemies taking the harvest (62:8) fits the hardship described in Haggai 1:6–11 and Nehemiah 5.
views.C: Chapter 62 continues 60–61 and reuses 40–55 heavily: the highway (40:3), the reward with him (40:10), the flag (49:22), Zion's marriage (54:1–8). Many critics take 62:10–12 as a deliberate echo of 40:1–11, framing 40–62 as a whole.
views.J: Jewish reading takes the chapter as the promise of the final redemption; 61:10–63:9 is the haftarah of Nitzavim, read on the Sabbath before Rosh Hashanah. The guards of 62:6 were read as angels, prophets or mourners for Zion.
views.X: Churches read 62:1–5 at Christmas and with the wedding at Cana (John 2:1–11), and hear 62:11 in Matthew's account of the entry into Jerusalem. Hymns about "Beulah land" made the chapter a picture of heaven.
views.F: Futurist readers expect the promises of 62:4–9 to be fulfilled in a restored, inhabited land of Israel in the age to come.

echoes: 40:1–11; 49:14–23; 54:1–8; 57:14; 60:14–15; 65:15; 2 Kings 21:1; Deuteronomy 28:33; Zephaniah 3:17; Matthew 21:5; Revelation 2:17; Revelation 3:12; Revelation 19:7

settings.what: A vow of persistent prayer and new names for Zion
settings.by: The prophet, perhaps continuing from 61:1–3, with the LORD's oath quoted (62:8–9)
settings.to: Jerusalem, addressed as a woman, and the watchmen and "remembrancers" who pray for her
settings.when: After the return from Babylon, before the walls were rebuilt (critical view); or Isaiah's vision for that time (traditional view)
settings.why: To answer Zion's sense of abandonment with God's delight, and to enlist others in pressing God to keep his promises. Knowing the city's emptiness and danger explains the stress on walls, guards, harvests and returning people.
settings.readers: Later readers sang the chapter as a love song between God and his people, and used its watchmen as a picture of prayer for Jerusalem and for the church.
views: Spoken in Judah in the late 500s BC (Westermann; Blenkinsopp).
Isaiah's vision of the far future, given in the 700s BC (Oswalt; Motyer).

title: The One Who Trod the Winepress
sum: A watchman sees a warrior coming from Edom, from Bozrah, his clothes stained red, and asks who he is. The answer is the LORD, "great at saving". Asked why his clothes are red, he says he has trodden the winepress alone, trampling the peoples in his anger, and their juice stained his garments. No one helped, so his own arm won the victory.

Then the mood changes. A long prayer begins (63:7–64:12). The speaker remembers the LORD's loyal love: how he saved Israel in the exodus, shared their distress, carried them, and gave them rest by his holy spirit, though they rebelled and grieved that spirit. Now the people ask where that God has gone. They plead with him as their Father and Redeemer, even if Abraham and Israel do not know them, and complain that their foes have trampled his sanctuary.
readings: Read as judgment on Edom
The first six verses are a victory poem about God's judgment on Edom, Judah's old enemy, and through Edom on all nations hostile to his people.
Read of Christ
Revelation 19:13–15 applies the image of the winepress and the stained robe to Christ. Many church fathers read 63:1–6 of the passion and the ascension.
Read as a lament
63:7–64:12 is a community lament, and one of the most moving prayers in the Bible. It moves from memory to complaint to confession and plea.

views.H: Edom moved into southern Judah after 586 BC and was hated for joining in Jerusalem's fall (Obadiah; Psalm 137:7). Edom itself was overrun by Arab peoples in the 500s–400s BC (Malachi 1:3–4). The lament of 63:7–64:12 assumes the temple still lies in ruins (63:18; 64:10–11).
views.C: Many scholars think the lament is one of the oldest parts of 56–66, written in Judah soon after 586 BC, perhaps close in time to Lamentations. 63:1–6 balances 59:15–20 around chapters 60–62.
views.J: Rabbinic tradition read Edom as Rome, and 63:1–6 as the final judgment on it. The Qere of 63:9, "in all their distress, he was distressed", was read with the rabbinic teaching that God's presence went with Israel into every exile (compare Bavli Megillah 29a).
views.X: Christians read 63:1–6 through Revelation 19, and many fathers saw in it Christ's passion and ascension. 63:16 and 64:8 are read in Advent, and 63:10 is cited for the Holy Spirit as a person.
views.F: Futurist readers take 63:1–6 as Christ's return in judgment (Revelation 19), often linked to a final battle in the region of Edom (Bozrah) in Jordan.

deep.h: The winepress from Isaiah to Revelation and the "Battle Hymn"
deep.b:
The image of God treading the nations like grapes runs from Isaiah through Joel to Revelation.

TextThe image
Isaiah 63:1–6The LORD returns from Edom, his clothes stained with the juice of the peoples he trod alone.
Lamentations 1:15The Lord has trodden Daughter Judah as in a winepress.
Joel 3:13The winepress is full and the vats overflow, for the nations' wickedness is great.
Revelation 14:19–20An angel throws the grapes "into the great winepress of God's anger", and blood flows out of it.
Revelation 19:13–15The rider "wears a robe dipped in blood" and "treads the winepress of the furious anger of God, the Almighty".

Julia Ward Howe wrote the "Battle Hymn of the Republic" in 1861 to the tune of "John Brown's Body". Its first verse, "He is trampling out the vintage where the grapes of wrath are stored", is taken from Isaiah 63 and Revelation 14. John Steinbeck took the title of The Grapes of Wrath (1939) from the hymn. In the Civil War, Union soldiers sang Isaiah's warrior as God's judgment on slavery.

echoes: 34:5–8; 59:15–20; 61:2; 51:9–11; Exodus 14–15; Exodus 23:20; Exodus 33:14; Deuteronomy 26:15; Deuteronomy 32:6; Psalm 77; Psalm 137:7; Obadiah; Ephesians 4:30; Revelation 14:19–20; Revelation 19:13–15

settings.what: A dialogue with the warrior from Edom
settings.by: A watchman's questions (63:1a, 63:2) and the LORD's answers (63:1b, 63:3–6)
settings.to: Judah, who had suffered from Edom's hostility and longed for God to act
settings.when: After the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC, when Edom had taken part in its ruin and moved into southern Judah (critical view); or Isaiah's vision (traditional view)
settings.why: To assure God's people that he has acted alone to judge their enemies and redeem them. Knowing Edom's role in 586 explains why Edom stands for every enemy.
settings.readers: Later readers saw in the warrior the Messiah judging Rome (Jewish tradition) or Christ in his passion and his return (Christian tradition).
views: Written in the late 500s BC, balancing 59:15–20 (Westermann; Blenkinsopp).
Isaiah's vision of God's final judgment, given in the 700s BC (Oswalt; Motyer).

settings.what: The opening of a community lament
settings.by: A speaker for the community, praying as "I" (63:7) and then "we"
settings.to: The LORD, addressed as Father and Redeemer
settings.when: In Judah while the temple lay in ruins, between 586 and 515 BC (most critical scholars); or Isaiah's prayer for that future (traditional view)
settings.why: To remind God of his past loyal love and to ask him to return. Knowing that the temple was burned and the people felt abandoned explains the prayer's bold questions.
settings.readers: Jews and Christians have prayed it in times of disaster. Its "our Father" shaped both the Jewish Avinu Malkenu and Christian prayer.
views: A lament from the ruins, perhaps the oldest part of 56–66 (Westermann; Williamson).
Isaiah's prayer on behalf of the future exiles (Oswalt).

title: A Prayer from the Ruins
sum: The lament that began in 63:7 continues. The people beg God to rip open the heavens and come down, as fire sets brushwood alight, so that the nations would tremble. They remember that no one has ever seen or heard of a God like him, who acts for those who wait for him. But they confess that God was angry and they went on sinning: all of them are like someone unclean, even their right deeds are like a cloth from a woman's monthly period, and their sins blow them away like leaves.

No one calls on God's name, for he has hidden his face. Yet they appeal to him again: "You are our Father. We are the clay, and you are the potter." They ask him not to be angry forever, and describe the ruins: Zion a wilderness, Jerusalem a desolation, the temple where their ancestors praised him burned with fire. The prayer ends with a question: will God hold back and stay silent?
readings: Read as a community lament
With 63:7–19 the chapter forms one of the great communal laments of the Bible, comparable to Psalm 44, Psalm 79 and Lamentations. It ends without an answer.
Read as confession of sin
64:5–7 is one of the strongest confessions in the Bible, and 64:6 became a central text in debates about human goodness and grace.
Read as a call for God's coming
The cry "rip open the heavens and come down" became a prayer for the coming of the Messiah, and the church sings it in Advent.

views.H: The burned temple and ruined cities (64:10–11) point to the time after 586 BC and before the temple was rebuilt in 515 BC. The prayer may come from the Judeans who stayed in the land.
views.C: Many scholars see 63:7–64:12 as an older lament, perhaps from the decades after 586 BC, taken into Third Isaiah and answered by chapter 65. Some (Hanson) read it as the voice of a marginalized group.
views.J: In Jewish reading the prayer expresses Israel's longing for redemption. 63:16 and 64:8 ("our Father") echo through the liturgy of the High Holy Days.
views.X: The Western church sings 64:1 in Advent ("O that you would rend the heavens"), and Paul's quotation in 1 Corinthians 2:9 made 64:4 a text about the hidden wisdom of God. 64:6 is central in Protestant and Catholic debate about good works.
views.F: Futurist readers sometimes take the prayer as Israel's future repentance before Christ's return (compare Zechariah 12:10).

traditions.q: The people say that "all our right deeds" are unclean (64:6). Does this mean that every good act of a sinner, or even of a believer, is sin before God?
views: No. The verse describes a people turned away from God, not the good works of those made righteous by grace. The Council of Trent taught that the justified do not sin in every good work and that their good works, done in grace, are truly good and meritorious (Session 6, canons 25 and 32).

Before faith, no work can make a person right with God, and even the good works of believers remain impure because of the sin that clings to them. They please God only for Christ's sake, by faith (Augsburg Confession 20; Apology 4).

Even "the very best we do in this life is imperfect and stained with sin", so no work can be the ground of being right with God (Heidelberg Catechism, Q. 62). The good works of believers are accepted because God looks on them in Christ (Westminster Confession 16.5–6).

Works done before grace cannot justify, but God's grace goes before and makes real good possible, and believers can grow toward holiness. The Articles of Religion say that good works after justification cannot put away sin, yet are pleasing to God in Christ (Article 10).

Orthodox teaching does not frame the question in legal terms. The verse shows human beings sick and in need of healing; salvation is a lifelong sharing in God's life, in which grace and human effort work together.

echoes: 63:7–19; 65:1; 29:16; 45:9; Exodus 19:18; Leviticus 15:19–24; Psalm 44; Psalm 74; Psalm 79; Lamentations 5:20–22; Mark 1:10; 1 Corinthians 2:9; Romans 9:20–21

settings.what: The second half of the community lament
settings.by: A speaker for the community, praying as "we"
settings.to: The LORD, addressed as Father and potter
settings.when: In Judah while Jerusalem and the temple lay in ruins, between 586 and 515 BC (most critical scholars); or Isaiah's prayer for that future (traditional view)
settings.why: To confess the people's sin honestly and still to plead with God on the ground of his fatherhood and his workmanship. Knowing the burned temple and empty cities explains both the despair and the urgency.
settings.readers: Readers have prayed this chapter in disaster and in Advent, and argued over 64:6 in the debates of the Reformation.
views: A lament from the ruins after 586 BC (Westermann; Blenkinsopp).
Isaiah's prayer for the exiles, seen ahead (Oswalt; Motyer).

title: New Heavens and a New Earth
sum: God answers the lament of chapters 63–64. He was ready to be found, holding out his hands all day to a rebellious people who sacrificed in gardens, sat among tombs, ate pork and told others to keep away because they were holy. He will repay them. But as a farmer spares a cluster with juice in it, he will spare his servants: they will inherit his mountains from Sharon to the Valley of Achor. Those who set tables for Luck and Fate will meet the sword.

The chapter then divides God's servants from the rest. The servants will eat, drink and rejoice; the others will go hungry and be ashamed. Then God announces that he is creating new heavens and a new earth and a Jerusalem of joy. There will be no more weeping or early death; people will live in the houses they build and eat from the vineyards they plant; God will answer before they call; and the wolf and the lamb will graze together on his holy mountain.
readings: Read as God's answer to the lament
The chapter replies point by point to 63:7–64:12: God was not silent; his people did not answer. Yet he will not destroy them all, and he will make a new beginning.
Read as a vision of the new creation
65:17–25 is the Bible's first vision of "new heavens and a new earth", taken up in 2 Peter 3:13 and Revelation 21. It shapes Jewish and Christian hope for the world to come.
Read as a picture of the millennium
Many premillennial readers take 65:20–25, where death still occurs, as a description of Christ's thousand-year reign (Revelation 20) rather than the eternal state.

views.H: The cults of 65:3–5 and 65:11 fit Judah after the return, where traditional and foreign practices continued alongside the rebuilt temple (compare Ezekiel 8; Zechariah 5). Long life, safe harvests and safe childbirth (65:20–23) answer the hardships of a small, struggling province.
views.C: Many scholars read 65–66 as a reply to the lament of 63:7–64:12 and as the latest layer of Isaiah, framing the book with chapter 1. The split between "my servants" and others is central to the theories of Hanson and others about conflict in early Persian Judah.
views.J: Rabbinic tradition read 65:17 of the world to come and the messianic age; Maimonides read the peaceful animals of 11:6 (repeated in 65:25) as a figure of peace among nations, not a change in nature (Laws of Kings 12:1). The chapter's peaceful animals are among the most quoted pictures of the messianic age.
views.X: Christians read 65:17–25 through 2 Peter 3:13 and Revelation 21–22 as the hope of a renewed creation. Paul cites 65:1–2 in Romans 10:20–21 for the faith of the Gentiles and the unbelief of many in Israel.
views.F: Premillennial and dispensational readers see 65:17–19 as the eternal state and 65:20–25 as the millennium, or read the whole passage as a millennial Jerusalem, because of death and sin in 65:20.

deep.h: New heavens and a new earth in Isaiah, 2 Peter and Revelation
deep.b:
Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22 are the only places in the Hebrew Bible that speak of "new heavens and a new earth". The New Testament takes the phrase up twice.

TextWhat is said
Isaiah 65:17–25God creates new heavens and a new earth and a joyful Jerusalem: no weeping, long life, safe homes and harvests, peace among animals.
Isaiah 66:22The new heavens and earth will stand, and so will the people's descendants and name.
2 Peter 3:10–13The present heavens will pass away with fire; believers wait for new heavens and a new earth "in which righteousness lives".
Revelation 21:1–5"Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth"; the sea is gone, the holy city comes down, and God wipes away every tear: "Look, I am making all things new."

The texts differ. Isaiah's picture keeps houses, vineyards and death at a great age; Revelation's has no death and no sea. Jewish writings between the Testaments develop the idea too: 1 Enoch 91:16 speaks of the first heaven passing away and a new heaven appearing, and the Qumran texts speak of "the new creation". Readers ask whether the new creation replaces the old world or renews it. Romans 8:19–22 speaks of creation itself being set free.

traditions.q: Isaiah 65:20 says people will still die, though at a great age. Does the passage describe the eternal new creation, or an earthly kingdom before it?
views: The death and sin of 65:20 show that the passage describes Christ's thousand-year reign on earth (Revelation 20), when Israel is restored and people live very long lives, before the final new heavens and earth. Isaiah sees both ages together, as a prophet sees mountain peaks without the valley between.

Divided. Many Reformed teachers are amillennial: the passage pictures the eternal new earth in the language of the present world, and death at a hundred is a way of saying that life will be full and long. Postmillennial Reformed teachers, such as Charles Hodge and Loraine Boettner, read 65:20 instead of a long golden age of the gospel within history, when most of the world turns to Christ, before he returns.

Historic premillennialists, such as George Eldon Ladd, also read 65:20–25 of an earthly reign of Christ after his return and before the final new creation, but without the dispensational separation of Israel and the church.

The Church rejects any earthly messianic kingdom before the end of history (Catechism 676) and reads the passage of the new creation: the universe will be renewed when the kingdom of God comes in its fullness (Catechism 1042–1047).
Orthodox teaching reads the passage of the age to come and the transfiguration of creation, and has generally rejected the idea of an earthly thousand-year kingdom (chiliasm).

Seventh-day Adventists teach that the millennium is spent in heaven while the earth lies empty; after it, God recreates the earth as the eternal home of the saved, the new earth of Isaiah 65 and Revelation 21 (Fundamental Beliefs 27–28).

settings.what: God's answer to the lament, dividing his servants from the rest
settings.to: The people of Judah, split between those who forsake the LORD for other rites and "my servants"
settings.when: After the return from Babylon, perhaps in the late 500s or 400s BC (critical view); or Isaiah's vision for that time (traditional view)
settings.why: To answer the complaint that God was silent: he called and was not answered. Knowing the mixed religious practice of post-exilic Judah explains the specific charges and the promise to spare the faithful.
settings.readers: Paul read 65:1–2 of the Gentiles and Israel. Later Jewish and Christian readers used the servants and the rebels as a picture of the faithful and the faithless in every age.
views: The latest layer of Isaiah, answering 63:7–64:12 (Westermann; Blenkinsopp; Stromberg).
Isaiah's prophecy for the future community (Oswalt; Motyer).

settings.what: New heavens, a new earth and a Jerusalem of joy
settings.to: His servants, the faithful in Judah
settings.why: To give a discouraged people a picture of life as God intends it: safe, long, fruitful and at peace. Knowing the infant deaths, lost harvests and insecurity of the time shows why these blessings are named.
settings.readers: Jewish readers heard the world to come and the messianic age; Christians, the new creation of Revelation 21 or the millennium of Revelation 20.
views: A poetic picture of a restored Jerusalem (many critical scholars).
A promise of cosmic renewal, fulfilled at the end (Childs; Oswalt).
A picture of Christ's earthly reign (Walvoord).

title: Heaven Is My Throne
sum: God says that heaven is his throne and the earth his footstool: no house can contain him. He looks instead to the poor and humble who tremble at his word. Those who mix sacrifice with murder and idolatry have chosen their own ways, and he will choose their punishment. The faithful, mocked and pushed out by their own brothers, are told that their enemies will be put to shame.

Zion gives birth without labor, and a nation is born in a day. All who love Jerusalem are called to rejoice and to nurse at her breast, and God comforts them as a mother comforts her child. Then the LORD comes in fire to judge. He gathers all nations to see his glory, sends survivors to the distant lands to tell of it, and takes some of them to be Levite priests. As the new heavens and earth will stand, so will the people's name; all flesh will come to worship. The book ends with the bodies of the rebels, whose worm will not die and whose fire will not be put out.
readings: Read as the book's conclusion

Chapter 66 gathers the themes of Isaiah: the temple and true worship (1:10–17), Zion's children, the nations streaming to Jerusalem (2:2–4), the servants and the rebels, and the new creation. Many scholars see 65–66 as framing the book with chapter 1.
Read as a vision of the nations
66:18–23 is one of the widest visions of the Hebrew Bible: all nations see God's glory, messengers go to the ends of the earth, and foreigners may serve as priests.
Read as a text about hell
The final verse, quoted by Jesus in Mark 9:48, shaped Jewish and Christian ideas of Gehenna and final punishment.

views.H: After the temple was rebuilt in 515 BC, disputes arose over who could serve in it and how worship was to be done (compare Malachi 1–2; Ezra 9–10). Some of chapter 66 may reflect those disputes; its foreign rites (66:3, 17) match the practices condemned in 65:3–5.
views.C: Most critical scholars take 66 as among the latest parts of Isaiah, perhaps written to close the whole book; 66:18–24 is often seen as a final addition. The chapter echoes chapter 1 at many points (1:2, 11–13, 28–31 and 66:3, 23–24).
views.J: The synagogue repeats 66:23 after 66:24 so that the book ends with worship rather than corpses. The Mishnah and Talmud use 66:23–24 in debates about the judgment of the wicked in Gehenna.
views.X: Stephen (Acts 7:49–50) and Jesus (Mark 9:48) quote the chapter. Christian readers have seen the church's mission to the nations in 66:18–21 and the doctrine of hell in 66:24.
views.F: Futurist readers see the chapter fulfilled in a future kingdom in which the nations worship in Jerusalem (66:23) and the wicked are judged (66:24).

deep.h: From the Valley of Hinnom to Gehenna
deep.b:
Isaiah's last verse describes corpses outside Jerusalem. Later readers connected it with the Valley of Hinnom on the city's south side, and through it with the idea of hell.

TextWhat it says
2 Kings 23:10Josiah defiles "Topheth, in the Valley of Ben-hinnom", so no one can sacrifice children there.
Jeremiah 7:31–33The valley will be called the Valley of Slaughter; corpses will lie there unburied.
Isaiah 66:24Rebels' corpses with an undying worm and unquenched fire, "a horror to all flesh".
1 Enoch 27:1–3An "accursed valley" by Jerusalem is the place of judgment for the cursed, seen by the righteous.
Judith 16:17God "will put fire and worms into their flesh, and they will weep and feel it forever".
Mark 9:43–48Jesus warns of Gehenna, "where their worm does not die and the fire is not put out".

The Greek Geenna comes from the Hebrew Ge Hinnom, "valley of Hinnom". In Isaiah the corpses are dead; the fire and worm consume bodies. Later texts make the punishment conscious and lasting. Readers still debate whether the images mean endless suffering, final destruction, or a purifying judgment; see the traditions card below. In Mark, the repeated lines (9:44, 46) are absent from the oldest manuscripts; only 9:48 is certain.

traditions.q: Jesus applies "their worm will not die, and their fire will not be put out" (66:24) to Gehenna. Does this mean that the punishment of the lost is endless and conscious?
views: Yes. The Church teaches the existence and eternity of hell, whose chief punishment is eternal separation from God; the images of fire express its reality (Catechism 1033–1035).

Hell is real and lasting, but is often described as the experience of God's love by those who refuse it: the same fire is light to the saints and burning to the unrepentant. Some Orthodox writers hope that all may yet be saved, without teaching it as doctrine.

Yes. The wicked "shall be cast into eternal torments, and be punished with everlasting destruction" (Westminster Confession 33.2), and the undying worm is often read of an endless conscience of guilt.

Anglican teaching affirms final judgment but leaves its nature open. The Church of England's Doctrine Commission described hell as total non-being rather than eternal torment, as the final choice of those who reject God.

No. The wicked will be destroyed and cease to exist. The fire is unquenchable because it cannot be put out until it has done its work, and Isaiah's verse describes corpses, not living sufferers (Fundamental Beliefs 26–27).
No. Gehenna is a symbol of eternal destruction with no hope of resurrection. The bodies in Isaiah 66:24 are dead, consumed by worms and fire, not tormented.

Most evangelicals hold to eternal conscious punishment, but a growing number, following John Stott and Edward Fudge, read the undying worm and unquenchable fire as final destruction (conditional immortality).

settings.what: True worship, a birth for Zion, and fire for the rebels
settings.to: The people of Judah, divided between those who "tremble at my word" and those who mock and exclude them
settings.when: After the temple was rebuilt in 515 BC, or as it was being rebuilt (critical view); or Isaiah's vision for that time (traditional view)
settings.why: To warn that a temple and its sacrifices mean nothing without humble obedience, and to comfort the faithful who were pushed out. Knowing the disputes over the rebuilt temple helps explain the sharp contrasts.
settings.readers: Stephen used 66:1–2 against trust in the temple. Jews and Christians alike took the "tremblers" as the model of humble faith.
views: One of the latest parts of Isaiah, reflecting disputes over the second temple (Hanson; Blenkinsopp).
Isaiah's word about true worship, for his day and the future (Oswalt; Motyer).

settings.what: All nations gathered, and the book's last scene
settings.to: Zion's people, and through them the nations
settings.when: The same setting as 66:1–17; many scholars think 66:18–24 was added to close the whole book
settings.why: To end Isaiah with God's glory among the nations, foreigners serving him, and lasting worship, but also with a warning that rebellion ends in ruin. The ending ties the book back to chapter 1.
settings.readers: Jesus' warning about Gehenna (Mark 9:48), the early church's mission to the nations, and the synagogue's custom of repeating 66:23 all grew from these verses.
views: Written to close the book of Isaiah (Childs; Stromberg).
The end of Isaiah's own prophecy (Oswalt).
